newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO join forces to restore calm in Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO join forces to restore calm in Hebron.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinian Authority joined forces to try to prevent clashes from erupting on Monday in the volatile West Bank streets of Hebron.
Witnesses said 200 Palestinian policemen stood on the invisible border dividing the 80 percent of the town handed over in January to PLO self-rule from the 20 percent still held by Israel.

Joint patrols resumed in the city, which has been a scene of almost daily unrest for more than two weeks. Troops have shot and wounded scores of Arabs hurling stones and fire bombs that wounded several soldiers.
Israel's Hebron brigade commander, identified for security reasons only as Colonel Gadi, told army radio his Palestinian counterparts had promised at a meeting on Sunday night to restore calm.
Arab shops previously closed by Israel were allowed to open.
"Last night there was a meeting between me and the Palestinian security establishment and police commanders in Hebron. This meeting took place at the request of the Palestinians," he said.
"They committed themselves to maintain the quiet in Hebron and asked us to...ease all sorts of steps we had taken recently in the city of Hebron," he said.

Israel had imposed measures he said were meant to bolster Israeli security -- closing off alleys, closing Palestinian shops and erecting roadblocks. Some 400 Jewish settlers live on the side still held by Israel.
"We decided this morning to begin with a small step and that's to allow (Palestinian) trade to open on two streets where trade had been closed near the Jewish Quarter," he said.
"We will see how this day ends and at the end of the day we'll evaluate the situation jointly with the Palestinians and we'll decide on the further steps."

Formal peace talks have been frozen since Israel broke ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem four months ago. The latest unrest was sparked by posters a Jewish woman put up in Hebron depicting Islam's Prophet Mohammad as a pig.
Israeli troops wounded 16 Arabs including five journalists during clashes on Sunday while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Palestinians they would pay dearly if violence continued.
The Israeli army denied it deliberately shot and wounded the five journalists, all Palestinians working in Hebron for foreign news agencies.

"It is against military policy to harm the media and whoever thinks the army deliberately shoots journalists slanders the Israel Defence Forces," the army said, suggesting cameramen ask officers to direct them to "less dangerous" vantage points.

Vice-Chairman Conny Mus of the Foreign Press Association told Reuters: "Our attitude right now is clearly to protest to the authorities to allow us to cover the events as we should and not make journalists working in the field a target."
Mus said it was "very clear the soldiers are not very happy with the camera people, especially the Palestinian camera people -- and I can't see this as a coincidence any more".
Clashes also erupted on Sunday near a Jewish shrine on the outskirts of Palestinian-ruled Bethlehem in the West Bank. No serious injuries were reported.
